```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(rscprep)
```

Two functions, in order. `diagnoseQC()` calculates the per-cell metrics that
filtering decisions get made from; `flagQC()` marks the cells those metrics
say are outliers. Neither one removes anything -- the split is deliberate, so
that you can look at what a threshold would cut before you cut it.

```{r, child = "_heart1k.Rmd"}
```

```{r, child = "_pseudo-samples.Rmd"}
```

The three depths matter here: they are what the per-sample section below is
about.

## Where this starts

This vignette picks up where [`mergeSeurat()`](mergeSeurat.html) leaves off.
With your own data that is:

```{r pipeline-real, eval = FALSE}
seurat_list <- seuratFrom10x(manifest = manifest)
seurat_list <- includeMetadata(seurat_list, sample_sheet)
seurat      <- mergeSeurat(seurat_list)
```

Here it is the pseudo-sample list:

```{r pipeline, results = "hide"}
seurat <- mergeSeurat(seurat_list)
```

```{r depths}
tapply(seurat$nCount_RNA, seurat$Ident, median)
```

Both functions want that single merged object rather than the list, so that
one set of thresholds is chosen from one view of the data.

## Calculating the metrics

```{r diagnose}
seurat <- diagnoseQC(seurat, organism = "mmu")
```

Three columns land in the metadata, alongside the `nCount_RNA` and
`nFeature_RNA` that Seurat already wrote:

```{r metadata}
head(seurat@meta.data[, c("nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA",
                          "pctMito", "pctRibo", "log10GenesPerUMI")])
```

* **`pctMito`** -- share of a cell's UMIs coming from mitochondrial genes.
  High means the cell lost cytoplasmic RNA through a ruptured membrane, so
  this is the usual first filter. What counts as high is tissue-dependent:
  5--10% is a common starting point, but cardiac, muscle and kidney are
  legitimately mitochondria-rich and a fixed cutoff throws away real cells.
  This is heart: `r round(100 * mean(seurat$pctMito > 10))`% of its cells are
  above 10%, and `r round(100 * mean(seurat$pctMito > 20))`% above 20%. (The
  gene subset inflates these somewhat -- see above.)
* **`pctRibo`** -- share from ribosomal protein genes. Rarely a hard filter,
  because it varies strongly by cell type. Useful as a comparison between
  samples that ought to look alike: a sharp shift points at something
  technical.
* **`log10GenesPerUMI`** -- library complexity, `log10(nFeature) /
  log10(nCount)`. Between 0 and 1 for real cells; low means a library
  dominated by few transcripts. Around 0.8 is a conventional floor.

The percentages come from matching gene **symbols** against organism-specific
patterns, so `organism` has to match the data.

## When the patterns match nothing

Get the organism wrong and both columns come back as zeroes. That is loud
rather than silent:

```{r wrong-organism}
wrong <- diagnoseQC(seurat, organism = "hsa")   # mouse data
```

The same warning fires when the organism is right but the matrix is still
keyed by Ensembl IDs, which is the other common cause -- `ENSMUSG00000064341`
matches no symbol pattern. Convert the rownames to symbols before diagnosing.

Four organisms are supported, differing only in the capitalisation convention
their symbols follow:

| code | organism | mito | ribo |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"hsa"` | human | `^MT-` | `^RP[SL]` |
| `"mmu"` | mouse | `^mt` | `^Rp[sl]` |
| `"rno"` | rat | `^Mt-` | `^Rp[sl]` |
| `"dre"` | zebrafish | `^mt-` | `^rp[sl]` |

An organism not listed can borrow the code of one whose convention it shares.

## Cell cycle, optionally

`doCellCycle = TRUE` also hands the object to `runCellCycle()`, adding
`S.Score`, `G2M.Score` and `Phase`. It is not run here, because for mouse
data it converts the human marker lists through `orthogene`, which needs
network access:

```{r cellcycle, eval = FALSE}
seurat <- diagnoseQC(seurat, organism = "mmu", doCellCycle = TRUE)
```

It is off by default because, unlike the metrics above, scoring assumes
normalised data -- and will run `Seurat::NormalizeData()` on the object itself,
with a warning, if it arrives raw. See `?runCellCycle` for the detail,
including the `method` argument for machines without network access.

## Flagging outliers

`flagQC()` marks cells that sit an unusual distance from the rest, using the
median absolute deviation rather than a fixed cutoff:

```{r flag}
flagged <- flagQC(seurat, metrics = c(nFeature_RNA = "lower", pctMito = "higher"))
```

Each entry is `column = bound`, and the bound is per metric because which tail
matters depends on the metric. `nFeature_RNA` wants `"lower"` -- the low tail
is empty droplets and dying cells, while the high tail is mostly real,
well-captured cells. `pctMito` wants `"higher"`, since high is bad and low is
not. `"both"` is the default, and is what you want when doublets are the
concern.

A MAD-based threshold adapts to the data, which a hard cutoff cannot: a
cutoff carried between experiments discards good cells from a shallow run and
keeps bad ones from a deep one. The cost is that it assumes most of the cells
it is estimated from are good. On a badly failed sample it will call the
failure normal and flag the survivors.

### When the log scale is wrong

Look at the `pctMito` line above: an upper cutoff of
`r round(getOutlierSummary(flagged)$upper[2])`%, which no cell can exceed.
The MAD is estimated on a log2 scale by default. That suits count metrics,
which are strongly right-skewed. But in this heart, `pctMito` runs from near
0 to `r round(max(seurat$pctMito))`%. On a log scale the cells near zero
stretch the spread so far that 3 MADs above the median lands past 100%.

On the original scale the cutoff is usable:

```{r flag-linear}
flagged <- flagQC(flagged, metrics = c(pctMito = "higher"), log = FALSE)
```

Check the thresholds in the console output before you trust the flags. A
cutoff outside the range a metric can take is the clearest sign the scale is
wrong for it.

## Estimating thresholds per sample

This is the argument that matters most. By default `flagQC()` estimates one
threshold across every cell in the object. If your samples differ in
sequencing depth -- and they usually do -- that single threshold describes
none of them.

The three pseudo-samples have median depths of roughly
`r knitr::combine_words(format(round(tapply(seurat$nCount_RNA, seurat$Ident, median), -1), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE))`
UMIs. Globally:

```{r global}
global <- flagQC(seurat, c(nFeature_RNA = "lower"))

table(global$Ident, flagged = global$nFeature_RNA_3_lower_outliers)
```

One cutoff, set mostly by the middle of the pooled data. It sits low for the
deep sample and high for the shallow one, so its flags land on `Sample_A`
because that sample was sequenced shallowly, not because its cells are worse.
The deep sample's poorest cells clear it easily.

Now per sample:

```{r grouped}
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(nFeature_RNA = "lower"), group_by = "Ident")

table(seurat$Ident, flagged = seurat$nFeature_RNA_3_lower_outliers)
```

Three thresholds instead of one, each set against its own sample's
distribution. The flags move to the cells that are poor *for their sample*,
which in this case means mostly the deep one. The console prints the *range*
across groups rather than a line per group, so a twenty-sample object stays
readable; the per-group numbers are in the summary table below.

`"Ident"` is the sample name `seuratFrom10x()` sets, but any discrete metadata
column works: a capture batch, a 10x lane, a tissue. Group on the technical
variable you want the threshold to absorb.

`pctMito` is a ratio, so it does not scale with depth the way `nFeature_RNA`
does, and depth is not a reason to group it. Flag it across all cells:

```{r mito-global}
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(pctMito = "higher"), log = FALSE)
```

## Reading the summary

Every call records what it did. `getOutlierSummary()` reads it back:

```{r summary}
qc <- getOutlierSummary(seurat)
qc[, c("metric", "group", "lower", "upper", "n_flagged", "pct_flagged")]
```

One row per metric per group. Two things to notice:

* Thresholds are on the **metric's own scale**, even though the
  `nFeature_RNA` estimate was made on a log scale. They can be compared
  against the column directly.
* The unenforced tail is `NA`, not an unapplied number. `nFeature_RNA` was
  flagged `"lower"` only, so its `upper` is blank rather than a cutoff nothing
  was tested against. The same applies to `n_lower` / `n_upper`.

Which group is losing the most cells?

```{r worst}
qc[order(-qc$pct_flagged), c("metric", "group", "n_flagged", "pct_flagged")]
```

The two calls above accumulated into this one table: `nFeature_RNA` per
sample, then `pctMito` across all cells. It is a record written at flag time,
not a live view -- cell counts describe the object as it stood then, which is
the point, since being able to say afterwards how many cells were dropped and
why is the reason to keep it.

## Groups too small to estimate from

Per-group estimation creates a failure mode global estimation does not have.
A group of two cells has no usable spread, and a group where over half the
cells share one value has a MAD of zero. Both are skipped rather than given a
meaningless threshold. Here, a made-up `Lane` column puts two cells in a lane
of their own:

```{r skipped}
lanes <- seurat
lanes$Lane <- ifelse(seq_len(ncol(lanes)) <= 2, "Lane_3",
                     rep(c("Lane_1", "Lane_2"), length.out = ncol(lanes)))

lanes <- flagQC(lanes, c(nCount_RNA = "lower"), group_by = "Lane")
```

One warning naming every skipped group, not one per group. Skipped groups
still get a row in the summary table, with `NA` thresholds and an `NA`
`column`, so nothing silently disappears.

That `NA`-not-`FALSE` distinction runs throughout. A cell is left `NA` when it
was never judged -- missing metric, missing `group_by` value, or a skipped
group -- so an unjudged cell is never mistaken for one that passed. It matters
at the filtering step below.

## Actually filtering

`flagQC()` writes logical columns and stops. Filtering is yours:

```{r filter}
flags <- grep("_outliers$", colnames(seurat@meta.data), value = TRUE)
flags

# `%in% TRUE` treats an unjudged NA as "not an outlier"; use `isTRUE`-style
# logic deliberately rather than letting NA propagate through `|`
keep     <- !Reduce(`|`, lapply(seurat@meta.data[flags], function(x) x %in% TRUE))
filtered <- seurat[, which(keep)]

table(seurat$Ident, keep)
```

Cross-tabulate before you subset. A sample losing far more than its
neighbours is worth understanding rather than filtering: it may have failed,
or it may be a genuinely different tissue where the thresholds do not
transfer.

You do not have to trust every flag. The columns are independent, so filter on
the subset you believe:

```{r selective}
filtered <- seurat[, which(!seurat$pctMito_3_higher_outliers %in% TRUE)]
ncol(filtered)
```

## Tuning

```{r tuning, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
# more aggressive
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(pctMito = "higher"), nmads = 2.5, log = FALSE)

# keep all but the extremes
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(pctMito = "higher"), nmads = 5, log = FALSE)

# a metric that is already symmetric does not want the log transform
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(log10GenesPerUMI = "lower"), log = FALSE)
```

```{r tuning-compare}
colSums(seurat@meta.data[grep("^pctMito_", colnames(seurat@meta.data))],
        na.rm = TRUE)
```

`nmads` is in the column name, so `nmads = 2.5`, `3` and `5` produce separate
columns and can be compared side by side. `group_by` is **not** in the name,
so re-running one metric with different grouping overwrites the previous flags
-- the summary table is updated to match, so it never describes a column that
is no longer there.

`log = TRUE` is the default and is right for count metrics, which are
right-skewed enough that the median and MAD are misleading on the raw scale.
Turn it off for anything already roughly symmetric, and for bounded metrics
like `pctMito` whose low end crowds against zero.

## Where this leaves you

```{r final, eval = FALSE}
seurat <- mergeSeurat(seuratFrom10x(manifest = manifest))
seurat <- diagnoseQC(seurat, organism = "mmu")
seurat <- flagQC(
  seurat,
  metrics  = c(nCount_RNA = "lower", nFeature_RNA = "lower"),
  group_by = "Ident"
)
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(pctMito = "higher"), log = FALSE)

getOutlierSummary(seurat)          # what would be cut, and from where
write.csv(getOutlierSummary(seurat), "qc/outlier_summary.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

Nothing has been removed at this point. The metrics are on the object, the
flags are on the object, and the record of how the thresholds were chosen is
on the object. Deciding what to drop is the next step, and it is a judgement
call -- which is why these functions stop short of making it.
